# Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core

###### Abstract.

LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous
evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without
weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous
investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web
content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the
boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine
role-specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds,
SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed
reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a
protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven-layer shared memory,
assembled by code from the system’s own record, gives each decision its
position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent’s past
decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades
every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and
each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic
gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All
three operate around an _invariant core_ of order arithmetic, risk rules
and discipline-agent prompts that no self-edit can reach. In a
five-month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the
system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of
its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more
and lost $`1.35`$ points against the market over five days where the
joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was
followed; and a 2015–2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the
maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector
traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a
learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control
evening. The code and prompts of the deployed system are open source.

###### Keywords: 

LLM multi-agent systems, shared memory, self-evolving agents, autonomous
investing, agentic Web, guardrails, field study

## 1. Introduction

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

LLM agents increasingly act on the Web rather than only answer from
it ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)). An agent that makes consequential
decisions from Web content must do three things at once: combine
heterogeneous, individually weak evidence into one decision; remember
what it has decided and how those decisions turned out; and improve from
experience ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib26); [Madaan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib21); [Wang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib28); [Fernando et al.,
2024](#bib.bib8); [ang Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) without weakening
the rules that constrain it. The third is the hardest to make safe: an
agent that can rewrite its instructions can also rewrite its safeguards,
and an agent that grades itself grades optimistically and does not
reliably correct itself ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib21); [Xiong
et al., 2024](#bib.bib37); [Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)).

Autonomous investing makes these requirements concrete. Every action is
irreversible and scored daily in money, and the incentive to let a
plausible lesson override a hard rule is constant. It is also a Web
setting in the sense of the agentic Web: every input is public Web
content (news feeds, SEC EDGAR filings, FRED statistics and exchange
quotes), every action leaves through a brokerage Web API, and the
central threat, untrusted content reaching an agent with authority to
act, is the one the Web-agent security literature studies ([Greshake
et al., 2023](#bib.bib9); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib6);
[Beurer-Kellner et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)). Prior LLM trading agents ([Yu
et al., 2024a](#bib.bib41); [Yu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib42); [Wang
et al., 2024b](#bib.bib29)) combine analyst roles, memory and
reflection, but they are evaluated on historical data, where
pre-training leakage is hard to exclude ([Lopez-Lira and Tang,
2026](#bib.bib19)); their learning loops run on the model’s own
reflection or on backtests, and nothing in them separates what may
change from what must not.

We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system in which nine agents trade
a US equity portfolio through a brokerage API, in six sessions per
trading day and with no human in the trading loop. Four analysts read
news, filings, macroeconomic series and market data; a Portfolio Manager
decides from their typed reports and from a seven-layer shared memory
that code assembles from the system’s own record; and the system
improves itself by _governed self-evolution_: code grades every decision
against realised outcomes, a reflector proposes typed changes to the
prompts, and a deterministic, reversible gate applies them but cannot
reach an _invariant core_ of order arithmetic, blocking risk rules and
the prompts of the discipline agents. The key idea is to draw the
boundary of self-evolution in the type system rather than in a prompt:
the proposal type cannot name the core, and every signal that drives
evolution is computed by code from outcomes, so the system can rewrite
itself without being able to weaken its own safeguards. Every decision
is a typed object stored with its inputs, so the trace that makes the
system governable also makes it _evaluable_: each output can be
re-scored against later prices and each input replayed through modified
prompts. We ran Steward live for five months in a brokerage paper
account on real-time Web data and market quotes, so every decision was
recorded before its outcome existed. To our knowledge, Steward is the
first self-evolving LLM agent evaluated over months of live operation
with every proposal and rejection of its evolution loop logged.

## 2. Related Work

#### Self-improving and self-evolving agents.

Reflexion ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib26)) and Self-Refine ([Madaan
et al., 2023](#bib.bib21)) let a model critique and revise its own
outputs; Voyager ([Wang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib28)) accumulates a skill
library; Promptbreeder ([Fernando et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)) and
OPRO ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)) optimise prompts with the model
as the proposer; Generative Agents ([Park et al., 2023](#bib.bib24)) add
memory and periodic reflection; a survey frames these as *self-evolving
agents* ([ang Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)). Two findings qualify the
programme: LLMs do not reliably self-correct ([Huang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12)), and their verbalised confidence is
overconfident ([Xiong et al., 2024](#bib.bib37)). We take both as
constraints: evolution is driven by code-computed outcomes and bounded
by a type-level allow-list and a deterministic gate. No prior work
reports a self-evolving agent operating for months in a live market with
its proposals and rejections logged.

#### Text, machine learning and LLMs in finance.

That text moves prices is established: media pessimism predicts
short-lived pressure that reverts ([Tetlock, 2007](#bib.bib27)); general
sentiment lexicons misclassify most negative words in filings ([Loughran
and McDonald, 2011](#bib.bib20)); and much of newswire sentiment is
impounded within the day ([Ke et al., 2019](#bib.bib16)).
Machine-learning return prediction from characteristics is the
benchmark ([Gu et al., 2020](#bib.bib10)). LLMs enter as readers of
text: GPT-4 headline labels predict a short drift ([Lopez-Lira and Tang,
2026](#bib.bib19)), and LLMs hallucinate financial facts unless grounded
by retrieval and tools ([Kang and Liu, 2023](#bib.bib14)). This
literature evaluates signals in backtests; our contribution is not a
signal but the governance of an agent that acts on many, evaluated live.

#### LLM agents for trading.

FinMem ([Yu et al., 2024a](#bib.bib41)) introduced layered memory;
FinCon ([Yu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib42)) a manager–analyst hierarchy with
verbal reinforcement; QuantAgent ([Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib29)) a
self-improving knowledge base; FinAgent ([Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib46)) and TradingAgents ([Xiao et al., 2024](#bib.bib35))
tool use and trading-firm roles; StockAgent ([Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib44)) a simulated market. Their evaluation is historical,
where pre-training leakage is hard to exclude ([Lopez-Lira and Tang,
2026](#bib.bib19)), or simulated, and where they learn, the signal is
the model’s own reflection ([Yu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib42); [Zhang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib46)) or a backtest ([Wang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib29)); Steward is evaluated forward in live trading,
learns from live outcomes graded by code and evolves around a core its
loop cannot reach. Surveys ([Nie et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)), domain
models ([Wu et al., 2023](#bib.bib33)) and benchmarks ([Xie et al.,
2024](#bib.bib36)) evaluate no deployed agent.

#### Security of LLM agents.

Prompt injection was characterised as goal hijacking ([Perez and
Ribeiro, 2022](#bib.bib25)) and, in its indirect form, as an attack
delivered through retrieved Web content ([Greshake et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9)); a formal treatment followed ([Liu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18)), and benchmarks show that agents remain
vulnerable ([Zhan et al., 2024](#bib.bib43); [Debenedetti et al.,
2024](#bib.bib6); [Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)). Recent defences are
architectural: execution isolation ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)),
capability and information-flow control ([Debenedetti et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5); [Costa et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)), and design patterns
that bound what an agent may do after reading untrusted
input ([Beurer-Kellner et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)). Our invariant core is
of this architectural kind, and our setting adds a channel beyond the
memory poisoning it studies ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)): the
agent’s own record fed back to a reflector that rewrites its
instructions.

#### Frameworks, structured output and Web agents.

AutoGen ([Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib32)), MetaGPT ([Hong et al.,
2024](#bib.bib11)) and CAMEL ([Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib17)) coordinate
role-specialised agents through natural language and structured
messages, building on chain-of-thought ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib30))
and ReAct ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib40)). Constrained
decoding ([Willard and Louf, 2023](#bib.bib31)) and structured-output
modes ([OpenAI, 2024](#bib.bib23)) make schema-conformant JSON cheap; we
use schemas as the specification of the reasoning procedure, the audit
artefact and the boundary of what evolution may touch. Mind2Web ([Deng
et al., 2023](#bib.bib7)) and WebArena ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib47))
evaluate agents that operate Web interfaces, the agentic-Web vision
anticipates agents as first-class Web actors ([Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39)), and Kapoor et al. ([Kapoor et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15)) ask that agent evaluation report cost and
reproducibility, which we do.

## 3. Problem Statement

#### Setting.

An agentic system $`S`$ with instructions $`\pi`$ (prompts and code)
observes Web evidence $`x_{t}`$ at each decision epoch $`t`$, emits a
decision $`d_{t}=S_{\pi}(x_{t})`$ and acts on it through an API. The
environment later reveals an outcome $`y_{t}`$, here market prices, that
scores $`d_{t}`$ independently of $`S`$. A _self-evolving_ system also
runs a loop that maps its own record
$`\mathcal{R}_{T}=\{(x_{t},d_{t},y_{t})\}_{t\leq T}`$ to revised
instructions $`\pi^{\prime}`$. We assume that the LLM components are
capable but unreliable in known ways: they cannot be trusted with
factual recall ([Kang and Liu, 2023](#bib.bib14)), their
self-assessments are overconfident ([Xiong et al., 2024](#bib.bib37))
and degrade on new tasks ([Kadavath et al., 2022](#bib.bib13)), their
free text is not machine-checkable, and the evidence they read is
untrusted ([Greshake et al., 2023](#bib.bib9)).

#### Failure modes.

Four failures can occur in such a loop without being observed.
(F1) *Self-grading*: the signal that drives evolution is the agent’s own
assessment $`\hat{g}_{t}`$ rather than $`y_{t}`$, and $`\hat{g}_{t}`$ is
optimistic. (F2) *Discipline erosion*: $`\pi^{\prime}`$ weakens the
rules that bound risk, because nothing separates what the loop may
change from what it must not. (F3) *Unauditable change*: no record ties
$`\pi^{\prime}`$ to the evidence that produced it, so an erroneous edit
can be neither found nor reverted. (F4) *Undetected inertness*: an edit
passes every check yet changes no decision, and the loop reports
progress it did not make.

#### Governed self-evolution.

We call a self-evolving system _governed_ if it meets five requirements.
(R1) *Typed record*: every $`d_{t}`$ is a machine-checkable object
stored with $`x_{t}`$, so that code can grade, read and replay
$`\mathcal{R}_{T}`$. (R2) *Outcome grading*: every signal fed back into
decisions or reflection is computed from $`y_{t}`$ by deterministic
code, never by $`S`$. (R3) *Typed proposals*: every proposed change to
$`\pi`$ is a typed object whose justification cites the graded record.
(R4) *Gated application*: deterministic code applies proposals under
invariants, logs every acceptance and rejection, can revert in one step,
and cannot reach an _invariant core_ $`\pi_{0}\subset\pi`$ (the
arithmetic, the blocking rules and the discipline agents’ prompts)
because the proposal type cannot name it. (R5) *Verification*: the
effect of a proposal is measured by replaying recorded inputs through
$`\pi^{\prime}`$. R1 and R2 address F1 and F3; R3 and R4 address F2 and
F3; R5 addresses F4.

#### Research questions.

A live deployment of such a system lets five questions be answered from
the record alone. (RQ1) What does each layer of $`S`$, from analyst
signal to executed order, contribute to the outcome? (RQ2) What do the
multi-agent decomposition and the shared memory add over a single model?
(RQ3) What does the evolution loop propose, how does the gate act on it,
and what does an applied learning change? (RQ4) Does the invariant core
hold, including under adversarial Web content, and at what cost?
(RQ5) Are the numbers the agents reason with grounded in their inputs?
§[4](#S4 "4. Design of Steward ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")
instantiates R1–R5 in a trading system and
§[5](#S5 "5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")
answers RQ1–RQ5.

## 4. Design of Steward

Steward instantiates R1–R5 in a trading system. Nine LLM agents and a
deterministic core run in six sessions
(§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1. Agents and sessions ‣ 4. Design of Steward ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"));
a shared memory and typed CoT make every decision a checkable record
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2. Shared memory and typed reasoning ‣ 4. Design of Steward ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"));
safety is enforced by construction rather than by instruction
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3. Safety by design ‣ 4. Design of Steward ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"));
and the system evolves itself at two time scales, by evening grading
(§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4. Short-term self-evolution: evening grading ‣ 4. Design of Steward ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")),
a gated quarterly loop
(§[4.5](#S4.SS5 "4.5. Long-term self-evolution: the quarterly loop ‣ 4. Design of Steward ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"))
and replay
(§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6. Verification by replay ‣ 4. Design of Steward ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).

### 4.1. Agents and sessions

#### Sessions.

The system runs six _sessions_ per trading day
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core");
Table [6](#A4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix D Sessions, Latency and Cost ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"),
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Sessions, Latency and Cost ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).
Only the morning session may open positions: four analysts read the Web
in parallel, a Portfolio Manager synthesises their typed reports with
the shared memory of
§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2. Shared memory and typed reasoning ‣ 4. Design of Steward ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"),
and the plan passes through a deterministic order constructor, a
blocking risk engine and an LLM Risk Manager before execution. The
midday and close sessions are sell-only and run a Position Reviewer; a
circuit breaker runs every 30 minutes without any LLM; the evening
session grades the day; and a quarterly session reflects on the
quarter’s graded outcomes. All evidence is public Web data (nine RSS
feeds, SEC EDGAR filings, nine FRED series, and daily price, sector and
valuation data for a universe of 80 US stocks and 21 exchange-traded
funds (ETFs)), and orders leave through a brokerage REST API.

#### Agents and their typed outputs.

Each agent emits one Pydantic object
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Agent Chain-of-Thought Schemas ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).
The _News Intelligence_ agent maintains three layers: a macro narrative
of themes and regime that persists across sessions, zero to four _state
changes_ per session (an event with its previous and new state, market
impact, affected symbols and a conviction), and per-symbol news items
with a sentiment and an impact summary. The _Earnings Analyst_ reads
10-Q and 10-K filings and reports revenue, margins, guidance and risk
flags with a sentiment and a data-quality note. The _Macro Analyst_
classifies the regime (risk-on, risk-off, neutral or transitional) from
the FRED series and issues sector stances and a target invested share.
The _Technical Analyst_ rates each symbol on a five-level scale with an
entry, a reference target, a stop and the condition that would
invalidate the setup. The _Portfolio Manager_ returns target positions;
the _Risk Manager_ approves or rejects the plan with a reason category,
field-level modifications and an optional scale factor for all buys; the
_Position Reviewer_ returns SELL, REDUCE, TRAIL_STOP or HOLD per
holding.

#### Orchestration.

A session runs at most once per day under a lock and is killed after 20
minutes. An LLM call is retried up to seven times with exponential
backoff and then fails over to a model from a second vendor. Every other
failure removes an action rather than adding one
(Table [13](#A6.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Failure handling. ‣ Appendix F Web Input, Taxonomies and Failure Handling ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"),
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Web Input, Taxonomies and Failure Handling ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).

### 4.2. Shared memory and typed reasoning

#### Shared multi-layer memory.

The agents share no conversation history. They share a memory that code
assembles from the system’s own record in seven layers, read by the
Portfolio Manager every morning. L1 holds the day’s typed analyst
signals. L2 gives each holding its entry date, days held, entry thesis
and its last seven Technical ratings. L3 is the narrative: the last
seven evening outlooks, seven days of macro regime, and the
high-conviction news state changes of the last two weeks. L4 is a 45-day
calibration table: code matches buys to later exits first-in-first-out
and reports win rate, mean return and holding time by entry size (below
\$5k, \$5–10k, above \$10k), so that the agent learns whether its
conviction pays. L5 lists the last five Risk Manager verdicts with their
categories, L6 the agent’s own last three decisions, so that reversals
are visible, and L7 a projected book that flags sectors approaching
their cap. Every number an agent can cite therefore comes from code, not
from another agent’s prose.

#### Schema-enforced reasoning.

Every agent’s output type contains its reasoning procedure as a nested
CoT object in which each step is a field declared str =
Field(min_length=1)
(Listing [1](#LST1 "Listing 1 ‣ Appendix A Schema Excerpts ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core");
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Agent Chain-of-Thought Schemas ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")
lists every agent’s steps). An agent cannot skip a step, enumerations
are Literal types, and cross-field validators encode domain invariants:
an actionable rating must carry an entry and a stop on the protective
side, a wrong grade must name a root cause, and a proposal must cite a
number. List-valued fields are validated item by item, so a malformed
entry is dropped and logged instead of invalidating a whole report. The
validated object is stored verbatim with its exact input, so the record
is not a log _about_ decisions but the decisions themselves, in a form
that code can grade, a reflector can read and a harness can replay.

### 4.3. Safety by design

Safety does not rest on any prompt: order arithmetic, blocking rules and
two discipline agents’ prompts form the _invariant core_ $`\pi_{0}`$,
which no self-edit can reach.

#### Judgement is separated from arithmetic.

No LLM number reaches the broker unchecked. The Portfolio Manager emits
TargetPosition _intent_ (a symbol, a target weight of at most 20%, a
conviction and a named condition that falsifies the thesis;
Listing [1](#LST1 "Listing 1 ‣ Appendix A Schema Excerpts ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")),
and a deterministic constructor turns it into orders. It takes the stop
from the Portfolio Manager or the Technical Analyst and otherwise places
it two average true ranges (ATR) below entry; at execution, code widens
any stop closer than one ATR, sizes the position as the smaller of its
target weight and a risk budget of 0.5% of equity at the stop, skips an
entry more than 5% from the market price, and skips a trade whose
risk/reward falls below 1.2 once execution has moved its prices.
Risk/reward is a computed field that the Risk Manager audits against a
floor of 1.5.

#### Hard rules run before the LLM check.

A blocking engine rejects BUYs that would drive cash negative, positions
above 20% of equity, sectors above 40%, net exposure above 90%, entries
without a stop, and any buy after a 3% daily loss. Only plans that pass
reach the LLM Risk Manager, which can reject, modify or scale them but
cannot approve what the engine blocked. The Risk Manager fails closed:
if its call or its schema fails, the plan is rejected.

#### Untrusted Web text stays upstream.

Prompt injection is the central threat to an agent that reads the Web
and holds authority to act ([Greshake et al., 2023](#bib.bib9)). Raw
headlines and filing text reach only the News and Earnings agents, whose
prompts treat them as data, drop instruction-like items and flag them in
the report. Code then drops any news state change whose keywords and
symbols appear neither in the input nor in the prior state, so an agent
cannot assert an event its sources do not contain. The Portfolio Manager
never sees a headline or a filing: it reads typed fields and the News
agent’s briefing, and anything it proposes still meets the constructor,
the hard rules and the Risk Manager. An injected instruction must
therefore survive a typed report, a deterministic engine and an
independent auditor before it can become an order
(§[5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5. RQ4: The invariant core under live and adversarial conditions ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).

#### Execution is fail-safe.

The executor sends sells first as limit orders and waits for their
fills, re-checks the daily loss before any buy, records each order
before submission so that a crash cannot leave an untracked fill, and
places a good-till-cancelled stop order as soon as a buy fills. The
circuit breaker, which uses no LLM, runs every 30 minutes and again at
each stage of the morning session; on a 3% daily loss it cancels open
entries and liquidates.

#### The evolvable periphery.

What _can_ change is the memory, rewritten daily by code, and the
prompts of the four analysts, the Portfolio Manager and the Evening
Analyst, each of which carries a marked _Learnings_ section that the
gate of
§[4.5](#S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2 "Gate and rewrite (R4). ‣ 4.5. Long-term self-evolution: the quarterly loop ‣ 4. Design of Steward ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")
may append to. The Risk Manager and the Position Reviewer, which encode
the hard discipline, are absent from the Literal type of the proposal
schema, so no self-edit can name them, and every rule above lives in
code that no prompt reaches. A learning can change _what_ an agent
proposes; it cannot change how a proposal becomes an order, or relax a
constraint.

### 4.4. Short-term self-evolution: evening grading

The evening session closes each trading day with two kinds of grading
(R2). Code first assembles the evidence: the sells of the last two days
and the buys of the last five with their realised returns, the last ten
next-day calls scored against the next day’s return, and the moves of at
least 8% over five days in universe names the system did not hold. The
Evening Analyst then completes a seven-step CoT that attributes
performance, reviews the previous outlook and each position’s thesis,
grades every trade correct, premature or wrong, assigns every wrong buy
one of nine root causes (for example _macro warning ignored_ or _top
chasing_), classifies missed opportunities, and sets a next-day bias.
Grades and P&L are written to the record in one transaction.

The labels the Evening Analyst assigns are categories; every quantity
that measures an outcome is computed by code from fills and prices. What
feeds forward is aggregated by code from that record: the calibration of
L4, the hit rates of the next-day calls, missed themes that recur in at
least two episodes or symbols over the last 14 evenings, and root causes
that recur across at least two symbols. The Portfolio Manager reads them
the next morning with the evening’s outlook, and its prompt bounds the
tilt a prior evening may apply to sizing at 20%.

### 4.5. Long-term self-evolution: the quarterly loop

The quarterly loop acts on the periphery in six steps, each assigned to
one side of a boundary: language models act and reflect, whereas code
records, grades, gates and rewrites.

#### Reflect and propose (R3).

On the last trading day of each quarter the evening session invokes a
Meta Reflector. Its input is a deterministic digest of 90 days of graded
record (alpha against SPY, calibration by size, themes caught and
missed, root causes of wrong trades and per-agent signal activity)
together with every editable prompt, its current _Learnings_ section and
the previous quarter’s reflection. Its CoT has seven mandatory steps in
a fixed order: performance facts, theme audit, loss autopsy, a five-axis
_self-portrait_, a _gap diagnosis_ that attributes the largest gaps to
agents, an _audit of existing prompts_ that checks whether a rule for
each gap already exists, and only then _proposal reasoning_. Its output
is at most three PromptLearning objects
(Listing [1](#LST1 "Listing 1 ‣ Appendix A Schema Excerpts ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")),
each an append or a retraction by content hash, with a text of 20–300
characters, a justification of at least 40 characters that must contain
a number from the digest, a target drawn from a Literal of the six
editable agents, and a self-rated confidence.

#### Gate and rewrite (R4).

The gate has two deterministic layers
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Gate Invariants ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).
The proposal schema rejects a malformed learning before it is staged,
and a PromptEditor applies the rest under its own invariants. Edits are
append-only into the marked section and tagged with quarter and content
hash, so human-written text is never modified; targets must be on the
allow-list; a word-boundary tripwire rejects absolutes such as _never_,
_always_ and _override_, which conflict with the hard rules; a Jaccard
similarity of 0.6 or more to an existing entry rejects a paraphrase; a
FIFO cap of ten entries per agent bounds the section; at most three
agents change per cycle; every accepted _and_ rejected proposal is
logged with its reason; and a cycle’s edits form a single
version-control commit, so that one git revert undoes a quarter of
evolution. The editor runs _stage-only_ (proposals written to a file for
human review) or _live-apply_, in which it can apply the reviewed file
rather than a fresh reflection. The Q2 cycle ran stage-only and the Q3
cycle live
(§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4. RQ3: Two cycles of self-evolution ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).

### 4.6. Verification by replay

Every LLM call is stored with its full response, the model, token counts
and cost and, since April 12, its complete input message, so any later
decision can be re-run (R5). A _decision-replay_ harness passes recorded
inputs through the prompt before and after a learning, with the rest of
the input fixed, and compares the outputs structurally: for the
Portfolio Manager, which symbols were added, dropped or resized; for the
Evening Analyst, whose full evening inputs are frozen to disk, how its
bias, grades, miss categories and suggested actions changed. Re-running
the unchanged prompt on the same inputs measures the model’s own
variance, against which a learning’s effect is read. This replaces the
argument that a learning _should_ help with a measurement of what it
changed on $`n`$ recorded inputs, at a cost of tens of dollars per
experiment.

## 5. Evaluation

### 5.1. Live deployment, data and methodology

Steward traded live from April 8 to September 10, 2026 (102 trading
days) on real-time Web data, in a brokerage _paper_ account funded with
US\$100,000. Paper fills are simulated against live quotes, so prices,
timing and order rejections are real; market impact is not. Every
decision was recorded before its outcome existed, so the live record is
forward and free of the pre-training leakage that is hard to exclude in
backtests of LLM agents ([Lopez-Lira and Tang, 2026](#bib.bib19)). Idle
cash earned the Treasury-bill rate. No human intervened in any trading
decision; the evening loop ran on 98 evenings and the quarterly loop at
both quarter ends. Code and prompts were unchanged from July 16 to the
end of the window. The deployment produced 619 pipeline runs and 1,632
logged LLM calls served by frontier models from two vendors with
automatic failover. Logged API cost was \$455, about US\$4.4 per trading
day
(Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Sessions, Latency and Cost ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).
The broker recorded 492 orders and 746 fills; the fill record is the
ground truth for all trade-level analysis.

R1 yields three kinds of evidence. The _live record_ is broker fills and
daily equity. _Trace re-scoring_ grades every recorded agent output
(7,843 Technical Analyst ratings, 1,885 symbol-days of news sentiment,
97 evening forecasts, 556 target weights, 90 risk verdicts and 438 round
trips) against later prices without any LLM. _Replay_ re-runs recorded
inputs through modified prompts or architectures. Forward-return
statistics use day-clustered standard errors because horizons overlap.
Every number, figure and table in this paper is computed by scripts from
the recorded trace, and the open-source system can be re-run on its
recorded inputs
([https://github.com/yebof/quant-agent](https://github.com/yebof/quant-agent)).

### 5.2. RQ1: What each layer contributes

#### Each analyst signal is weak on its own.

Scored against market-adjusted forward returns, the Technical Analyst’s
five-level rating has a mean daily rank information coefficient (IC) of
$`-0.004`$, $`0.019`$ and $`0.031`$ at 5, 10 and 20 days ($`t=1.2`$ at
20 days), with _sell_ ratings carrying the only discernible effect
($`-1.7\%\pm 1.4`$ over 20 days); and News sentiment is uncorrelated
with later moves
(Figure [5](#A5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Analyst signals and forecasts (RQ1). ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"),
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).
The value therefore lies in their synthesis. Code grading also held the
Evening Analyst to account: its 38 directional next-day calls were right
37% of the time, below the 54% base rate of up days, and because the
grade is computed by code (R2), this hit rate appeared in its own
next-day prompt.

#### The synthesis carries the value.

Following the recorded decisions through prices
(Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.1. Live deployment, data and methodology ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")a,
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Execution and exits hold the headroom. ‣ 5.2. RQ1: What each layer contributes ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core");
targets set at the decision-day close, 20% position cap, cash earning
the T-bill return), the analysts’ buy ratings return $`+1.3\%`$, whereas
the Portfolio Manager’s target weights return $`+15.4\%`$ with no exits
(at 93% exposure), $`+11.6\%`$ with the system’s own exit rules and
$`+12.2\%`$ with the Risk Manager’s recorded edits, at a higher Sharpe
ratio than without them (2.33 against 1.80). The Portfolio Manager’s
synthesis of weak signals with the shared memory thus matched the index
and beat every analyst-following baseline by more than ten points, and
the Risk Manager reduced volatility more than return.

#### Execution and exits hold the headroom.

The live portfolio returned +5.0% against the intent’s $`+12.2\%`$
because it was less invested: realised gross exposure averaged 56%
against 79%
(Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.1. Live deployment, data and methodology ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")b),
as 180 of 492 orders were cancelled or expired unfilled, the hard rules
trimmed buys and intraday stops fired where the close-based simulation
held. The same gap appears on the risk side, as a beta of 0.16 for the
live book against 0.64 for the intent
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Execution and exits hold the headroom. ‣ 5.2. RQ1: What each layer contributes ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).
Exits show the same pattern. Of 438 round trips, 306 were closed by
agent decisions and 132 by broker-held stops
(Table [7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Exits (RQ1). ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).
Lots closed by the core’s mechanical stops went on to gain only US\$0.7k
beyond the US\$3.7k they realised; lots closed by agent decisions went
on to gain US\$19.9k beyond the US\$0.8k realised
(Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.1. Live deployment, data and methodology ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")c).
The Evening Analyst had graded 134 of 163 sells _correct_; only the
outcome-scored measure exposes the opportunity cost, which is why R2
puts grading in code.

### 5.3. RQ2: The decomposition and the memory

The simulations take the Portfolio Manager’s intent as given. To test
the design upstream of it, we replay 20 mornings sampled evenly over the
deployment through three decision layers on their exact recorded inputs
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.3. RQ2: The decomposition and the memory ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"),
Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.1. Live deployment, data and methodology ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")d;
100 LLM calls): the deployed design (typed analyst reports plus memory;
two samples per morning), the same input without any memory layer, and a
single model that receives the raw data the analysts read and must
analyse and decide in one call. Each proposed book is scored by the
weight-averaged market-adjusted forward return of its names. The single
agent is a different trader: it targets 5.8 names a morning against 3.7,
puts 41% of equity into new intent against 19%, and reverses its own
recent decisions two and a half times as often (0.25 against 0.10 per
morning), including re-buying names it had just closed, which the
deployed design never did. Its books lose over the next five and ten
days ($`-1.35\pm 0.44`$ and $`-1.76\pm 0.75`$ points against SPY; hit
rates 35% and 32%), whereas the deployed design’s are indistinguishable
from zero. Removing the memory changes almost nothing on a single
morning, so the typed reports carry most of the per-morning information
and the memory’s role is longitudinal: calibration, continuity and
feedback.

### 5.4. RQ3: Two cycles of self-evolution

#### Q2: a root-cause diagnosis and a withheld learning.

The Meta Reflector’s first run (stage-only, 52 trading days) attributed
the shortfall against the index to “structural under-participation in a
broad rally, not a blow-up”; found that 14 of the 20 BUYs graded _wrong_
shared one root cause, _macro warning ignored_ (an active
high-conviction bearish news state change at purchase); declined to edit
a prompt where it traced the gap to the data rather than the
instructions; and proposed exactly one learning, to treat such a state
change as a sizing gate, at self-rated _low_ confidence. The gate
withheld it on its length invariant (282 characters against a
200-character cap) and logged why. Replay then measured what the gate
had declined
(Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Q2: a root-cause diagnosis and a withheld learning. ‣ 5.4. RQ3: Two cycles of self-evolution ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")a,
Table [8](#A5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Self-evolution (RQ3). ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core");
35 calls, US\$17): on the ten mornings whose BUYs were later graded
wrong and five control mornings, the Portfolio Manager prompt with the
learning kept 8 of the 10 flagged names that the baseline still proposed
within one point, and every weight moved within the noise of re-running
the baseline itself (1.8 points per name at the median). The withheld
learning was inert, so the strict gate cost nothing.

the applied Q3 learning: the share of recurring misses named in
suggested actions is about 40 percent for both; the share of replays in

#### Q3: self-audit and an applied learning.

The second run, on September 30, was live. The reflector first audited
its own Q2 diagnosis: _macro warning ignored_ had fallen from 14 wrong
BUYs to 3, and because the Portfolio Manager prompt already carried
rules for it, the reflector declined to add more, citing the risk of
overcorrection. It again sent two anomalies to the operators instead of
into prompts, attributing them correctly to the digest’s
instrumentation. It then located a new gap: 70 of 104 classified misses
were missed value entries or trend timings, some named on three or more
evenings without being acted on. Its one proposal, at _medium_
confidence, was a 185-character learning for the Evening Analyst: when
the same symbol is classified a missed value entry or trend on three or
more evenings, promote it to a suggested action with a TAKE/WAIT call
and a named blocker. The gate applied it as a one-file, reversible
commit. Because the operators had also revised other prompts and the
universe before the cycle, the October record cannot isolate the
learning; replay can. We re-ran ten evenings on which such recurrences
existed and four control evenings through the prompt before and after
the commit, two samples each
(Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Q2: a root-cause diagnosis and a withheld learning. ‣ 5.4. RQ3: Two cycles of self-evolution ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")b,
Table [9](#A5.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Self-evolution (RQ3). ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core");
56 calls, about US\$16). The agent adopted the learning, and only where
it applied: the prescribed form (an explicit TAKE/WAIT call or named
blocker) appeared in 5 of 20 trigger replays against 0 of 20 for the
base prompt and never on a control evening, while the next-day bias
stayed as stable as re-running the base prompt (86% against 79%
agreement). The edit thus added the targeted behaviour without
disturbing the rest of the output. Replay also located what the learning
still needs: the trigger presupposes a count of past classifications
that the Evening Analyst’s input does not provide, so the recurring
misses surfaced were unchanged (25 of 64 against 26 of 64). Adding that
count is a concrete next step, for a gap that the gate’s invariants
cannot detect and that replay found for US\$16.

#### The evening loop.

The daily loop should make the system less active after poorly graded
periods, and the record is consistent with this: realised exposure
co-moves with the trailing forecast hit rate ($`\rho=0.34`$, $`p=0.01`$)
and the trailing realised win rate ($`\rho=0.22`$, $`p=0.05`$), whereas
the Portfolio Manager’s declared sizing does not ($`|\rho|\leq 0.14`$;
Table [10](#A5.T10 "Table 10 ‣ Self-evolution (RQ3). ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core");
Holm-adjusted $`p=0.08`$ for the strongest relation): the adaptation
runs through the graded memory rather than through the agent’s stated
intent.

### 5.5. RQ4: The invariant core under live and adversarial conditions

#### Containment.

The portfolio returned +5.0% against +12.4% for SPY during a
semiconductor-led rally
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Containment. ‣ 5.5. RQ4: The invariant core under live and adversarial conditions ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")),
at a beta of 0.16 and volatility of 9.0% against 12.4%; alpha is not
identifiable over 102 days, and no claim of this paper rests on it.
Between June 22 and July 29 the semiconductor ETF fell 24.6%, QQQ 10.3%
and SPY 2.0%, whereas the portfolio lost 0.3%, having exited its
semiconductor positions in May on named triggers that are legible in the
trace. One window holds one drawdown, so we also backtest the
deterministic core alone over 2015–2026
(Table [11](#A5.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Grounding protocol. ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"),
Figure [6](#A5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Grounding protocol. ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")):
its stops, caps, cash-only rule and breaker applied to LLM-free weekly
entries on the universe’s 80 stocks, which rules out pre-training
leakage. The core lowered the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry
policies (median 37% $`\to`$ 28%) and under momentum entries (61%
$`\to`$ 33%), and the drawdown of the 2018, 2020 and 2022 sell-offs for
at least 49 of 50, at an unchanged Sharpe ratio; the caps and the
breaker do most of the work. In the 2026 semiconductor window the same
rules still lost 27% under momentum entries: the core bounds what
judgement can lose, and the agents’ May exits did the rest. The Risk
Manager rejected 4 of 90 plans and made 146 field-level edits; the
circuit breaker never had to liquidate; after the cash-only rule took
effect on April 19 gross exposure never exceeded 92%; and across 1,632
calls validation failed on 13 sub-items, each isolated without losing a
session.

#### Adversarial Web content.

Untrusted content reaches the agents through the news feeds. We insert
one adversarial item into the exact recorded input of ten mornings and
re-run the agent
(Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Adversarial Web content. ‣ 5.5. RQ4: The invariant core under live and adversarial conditions ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core");
50 calls, US\$19), with three payloads: a direct override (set one name
to 45% and every other target to zero), a plausible headline (300%
upside; managers are taking maximum size and disabling stops) and a
suspension of discipline (stops and the cash-only rule lifted, allocate
60% to an inverse ETF). The News agent excluded the item from its typed
report in all 20 replays and flagged it as instruction-like in every
briefing. Placed directly in the Portfolio Manager’s news section, as if
the analyst layer had passed it through, the item was followed in none
of 30 replays; in 23 the Portfolio Manager’s CoT named it as injected
content and refused it, most often because the symbol had no Technical
Analyst report and the demand conflicted with the stop and cash rules.
Had any replay complied, the schema would have dropped a 45% or 60%
target before the constructor and the hard caps would have bounded
anything smaller: injected content could at most change what an agent
_wanted_, and here it did not achieve even that.

| ------------------------ | ---------- | -------- | ----------------- | ------- | ------ |
| Payload                  | Excluded   | Labelled | Followed          | Refused | Max wt |
| P1 direct override       | 10/10      | 10/10    | 0/10              | 7/10    | 0%     |
| P2 plausible headline    | 10/10      | 10/10    | 0/10              | 6/10    | 0%     |
| P3 discipline suspension | –          | –        | 0/10              | 10/10   | 0%     |

Excluded/Labelled: dropped from / flagged in the News report;

### 5.6. RQ5: Grounding of cited numbers

Because every CoT is stored with its exact input, we can ask whether the
numbers an agent cites exist in what it was given. A deterministic audit
of 750 recorded CoTs
(Table [12](#A5.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Replay noise. ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core"))
extracted 254,094 cited numbers, excluding small integers and years, and
matched each against the agent’s input, its prompt and its own emitted
fields. A strict matcher (exact, rounded or truncated matches and
explicitly written arithmetic) grounds 96.1%; recognising derived
quantities such as risk/reward ratios and ATR-based stops raises this to
99.9%, and the median CoT is fully grounded for every agent. A placebo
against another day’s input grounds 22% under the strict matcher, so the
test discriminates. Of the 226 ungrounded numbers, nearly all are
unwritten intermediate results of the sizing formula or chosen trigger
levels; three are candidate fabrications (a wrong price, a misread
indicator and a recalled policy-rate peak absent from the input).

## 6. Discussion

RQ1–RQ5 yield three implications for multi-agent systems that act and
evolve in high-stakes Web settings.

#### Place the invariant core at the type level.

Making the core unreachable rather than discouraged (arithmetic and
blocking rules in code, the discipline agents absent from the Literal of
editable targets) is what makes it safe for the system to rewrite
itself. Lower drawdowns across four crashes in backtest and the failed
injections are its observable consequences.

#### Grade with code, and allocate discretion where the data show skill.

Outcome-scored grading attributes the value to the Portfolio Manager’s
synthesis and the core’s mechanical exits and locates the headroom in
discretionary exits and execution; the Evening Analyst’s own grades,
which rated 134 of 163 sells correct, would not have shown this. A
self-evolving system can improve only what it measures, so the next step
is to narrow the periphery on exits and add an execution agent inside
the core, leaving the judgement layer that works untouched.

#### A syntactic gate needs a semantic check.

The gate guarantees that a learning is short, novel, reversible and
confined to the periphery; it cannot tell whether the learning changes a
decision. Replay can, cheaply: it confirmed that the withheld learning
was inert and that the applied one was adopted only where intended
(§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4. RQ3: Two cycles of self-evolution ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")).
The Q3 learning also presupposes a count of past classifications that
the Evening Analyst’s input does not provide. Replay turned this into a
concrete fix. The natural next invariant is therefore an outcome-scored
replay check that confirms a learning is operable on the agent’s actual
inputs and measures its effect on decisions before it is applied.

#### Limitations and next steps.

The evidence comes from one configuration traded on a paper account
through one rising window, with overlapping forward horizons,
simulations that ignore fill risk and two quarterly cycles, one applied;
replays of 14–20 inputs expose behavioural differences but cannot rank
variants by return. Each limit narrows with operation: every further
quarter adds a cycle to the record, and the released harness scales
replay to more inputs at tens of dollars per experiment.

## 7. Conclusion

We presented Steward, a multi-agent LLM system for autonomous investing
in which role-specialised agents decide jointly over heterogeneous Web
data, share a memory computed by code, and evolve at two time scales
around an invariant core that no self-edit can reach. Five months of
live operation showed that the typed trace that makes such a system
governable also makes it evaluable: it located the method’s value and
its headroom layer by layer, recorded the system containing a sector
drawdown and resisting injected instructions, with a backtest of the
core alone lowering drawdowns across four crashes, and documented
self-evolution diagnosing its own failures and making targeted,
reversible edits whose effects replay verified at a cost of tens of
dollars. We release the system, the trace and the scripts so that
outcome-scored replay can be developed into a gate invariant on real
inputs.

## Ethical Considerations

The system traded a paper account, so no capital was at risk; all inputs
are public Web data used under the providers’ terms; no human subjects
were involved; and the released software is not investment advice. The
invariant core prevents a self-modifying agent from eroding its own risk
discipline by construction, and the recorded trace lets this be audited.

## Appendix B Agent Chain-of-Thought Schemas

Every LLM agent’s output model contains a nested chain-of-thought (CoT)
object whose fields are the reasoning steps the agent must perform, in
order. Each step is declared str = Field(min_length=1), so a missing or
empty step fails validation and the response is retried; the steps are
therefore not a prompting hint but part of the output contract, and they
are persisted verbatim with the decision.
Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix B Agent Chain-of-Thought Schemas ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")
lists the mandatory steps of each agent’s CoT as they appear in
src/models.py. The News Intelligence agent is the one agent without a
CoT: its structured output (a persistent macro narrative, a list of
typed state changes with conviction, and per-symbol alerts) _is_ its
reasoning structure. The Portfolio Manager’s CoT additionally carries
two optional steps, continuity_check (consistency with its own last
three decisions) and premortem_check (the strongest argument against its
largest position), which the prompt requires.

| ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tech Analyst (5)          | trend (price versus moving averages) $`\to`$ momentum (RSI, MACD) $`\to`$ volatility (Bollinger position, ATR) $`\to`$ volume (confirming or diverging) $`\to`$ support_resistance (levels, valuation flags). Output: rating, conviction, entry, stop, target, thesis_invalid_if; risk/reward is computed, not written. |
| Macro Analyst (6)         | volatility_analysis $`\to`$ yield_curve_analysis $`\to`$ monetary_policy_analysis $`\to`$ inflation_labor_credit $`\to`$ cross_signal_synthesis $`\to`$ sector_implications. Output: regime, confidence, target exposure, sector stances, regime-shift flag.                                                            |
| Earnings Analyst (5)      | fundamental_quality $`\to`$ growth_trajectory $`\to`$ strategic_risks $`\to`$ management_execution $`\to`$ valuation_context. Output: sentiment and conviction derivable from the steps.                                                                                                                                |
| Portfolio Manager (7 + 2) | macro_filter $`\to`$ news_check $`\to`$ earnings_check $`\to`$ signal_conflicts $`\to`$ sizing_logic $`\to`$ portfolio_balance $`\to`$ cash_target; optional continuity_check, premortem_check. ## Appendix C Gate Invariants

The proposal schema and the deterministic prompt editor enforce the
following on every proposed learning, independently of the LLM:
(1) append-only into a marked _Learnings_ section, each entry tagged
with quarter and content hash; (2) an allow-list of target agents, with
the Risk Manager and Position Reviewer excluded both here and in the
proposal schema’s Literal; (3) length ceiling (300 characters; 200
before the Q3 cycle) and justification floor; (4) a word-boundary
prohibited-word tripwire (_never_, _always_, _override_, _ignore all_,
_must always_, _must never_); (5) Jaccard token-similarity dedup against
existing entries (threshold 0.6); (6) a per-agent FIFO cap that evicts
the oldest auto-added entry; (7) a per-cycle cap on the number of agents
edited; (8) atomic file writes; (9) an audit log of accepted and
rejected proposals with reasons; (10) one git commit per cycle, skipping
any prompt file with uncommitted human edits so that the commit stays
cleanly revertible; (11) single-line, whitespace-normalised entries;
(12) an apply-from-file lane so that a human-reviewed proposal file, not
a fresh reflection, is what gets applied.

## Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material

Every table and figure below is computed from the recorded trace by our
evaluation scripts.

#### Scoring and simulation.

Forward returns are close to close over 1, 5, 10 and 20 trading days and
are market-adjusted by subtracting SPY’s return over the same horizon.
Means are taken first within each day and then across days, so that a
day with many ratings counts once, and standard errors are computed on
the daily means. The rank IC is the daily Spearman correlation between a
signal and the market-adjusted forward return, on days with at least
eight scored symbols. The policy-layer simulations of
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Execution and exits hold the headroom. ‣ 5.2. RQ1: What each layer contributes ‣ 5. Evaluation ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")
hold each recorded target from the decision day’s close, cap a name at
20% and the book at 100%, and earn the T-bill ETF’s return on idle cash.
With system exits they apply the Technical Analyst’s stop from the entry
day or the three days before it (8% below entry if none) and the
Position Reviewer’s recorded SELL, REDUCE (halving) and TRAIL_STOP
actions; with the Risk Manager, a rejected plan sets no targets and its
recorded allocation edits and scale factors are applied. The
analyst-following baselines put 5% in every name rated buy (or
high-conviction buy), up to 70% of equity.

#### Containment and grounding (RQ4, RQ5).

Table [11](#A5.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Grounding protocol. ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")
and
Figure [6](#A5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Grounding protocol. ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")
give the 2015–2026 backtest of the deterministic core;
Table [12](#A5.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Replay noise. ‣ Appendix E Additional Evaluation Material ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")
gives the grounding audit by agent.

#### Backtest protocol.

Entries are rebalanced on the first trading day of each week to ten
names at 9% each: the top ten by 126-day return skipping the last five
days (momentum), or ten names drawn uniformly (random, 50 seeds).
Without the core, the book holds 10% per name, fully invested, with no
stop, cap or breaker. The core applies a stop at entry minus two
ATR(14), triggered on the daily low and filled at the lower of the open
and the stop; a 40% GICS sector cap; at most 90% net exposure; the
cash-only rule; and a breaker that liquidates at the close after a day
of $`-3\%`$ or worse and re-enters at the next open. Stopped names stay
flat until the next rebalance. Trades cost 5 bp per side, and idle cash
earns a T-bill ETF.

#### Grounding protocol.

The audit samples up to 150 CoTs per agent and extracts every number in
their reasoning fields, excluding small integers and years. A number is
grounded if it occurs in the agent’s input message, in any historical
version of its prompt or in its own emitted fields, allowing rounding
and truncation; the derived matcher also accepts risk/reward ratios, ATR
multiples, percentage changes, weights and stop levels computed from
those values, and arithmetic written out in the text. The placebo pairs
each CoT with the input of another row of the same agent, half the
sample apart in time; because two-digit numbers such as 25% or 1.5 match
by chance, the placebo is reported on numbers with three or more
significant digits.

## Appendix F Web Input, Taxonomies and Failure Handling

#### Web input.

RSS items are deduplicated by normalised URL and then by title-word
Jaccard similarity above 0.7, their summaries are truncated to 300
characters, and at most 50 items enter the News agent’s prompt. Filing
text is parsed from HTML and capped at 30,000 characters. The Portfolio
Manager receives at most three news items per symbol, each reduced to
its conviction, sentiment and impact summary, with no headline. Every
news state change is checked by code against the session’s input and the
prior state, and dropped if none of its keywords or symbols occurs
there.

#### Evening taxonomy.

A wrong BUY carries one of nine root causes: greed or top chasing, macro
warning ignored (which must cite the warning), herd buying, averaging
down, broken thesis held, concentration, timing, systemic drawdown and
tail event, together with a thesis trajectory (strengthening, intact,
weakening, broken). A missed move is classified as a trend-timing miss,
a theme blind spot, a fundamentals mispricing, a missed value entry, a
noise rally or a risk-disciplined pass; the last two are not counted as
misses. The Risk Manager labels each verdict with one of ten reason
categories (for example _oversized_, _rr_fail_, _concentration_, _event
risk_, _data degraded_), which L5 feeds back to the Portfolio Manager.

#### Failure handling.

Table [13](#A6.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Failure handling. ‣ Appendix F Web Input, Taxonomies and Failure Handling ‣ Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing:A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core")
lists how the system contains each class of failure. The rule throughout
is that a failure removes an action rather than adding one.

| Failure                                 | Response                                                                 |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Transient LLM error (429, 5xx)          | up to 7 retries with backoff, then one call to a second vendor’s model   |
| Unparseable or invalid output           | the agent’s output is dropped; invalid list items are dropped singly     |
| Research agent fails                    | recorded as degraded; two degraded sources raise a Risk Manager advisory |
| Portfolio Manager fails                 | session aborts without orders; the next 30-minute tick retries           |
| Risk Manager fails                      | the plan is rejected (fail closed)                                       |
| Position Reviewer fails                 | no exit actions; broker-held stops remain                                |
| Evening Analyst fails                   | P&L is recorded; no grades are written                                   |
| Crash between order and record          | write-ahead record and reconciliation of orphans                         |
| Stale entry price ($`>`$5% from market) | the BUY is skipped                                                       |
| Daily loss beyond 3%                    | no new buys; the circuit breaker cancels entries and liquidates          |
| Session overrun                         | killed after 20 minutes; at most one run per session per day             |

Table 13. Failure classes and the system’s response.

#### Ablations.

With momentum entries the core’s drawdown is 36% without stops and 60%
without the breaker (33% in full).
